faq.a: DNA can be damaged by ultraviolet light from the Sun, some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, radiation, and normal reactions inside the cell. Mistakes also happen when DNA is copied.

faq.q: How does a cell find damaged DNA?
faq.a: Repair proteins move along the DNA, sensing places where the shape is wrong or a letter is mismatched. When they find one, they call in other proteins to fix it.
asks: How do cells check their DNA?

faq.q: How can the cell rebuild missing DNA?
faq.a: Because DNA has two matching strands, A always pairs with T and C with G. After the damaged section is cut out, enzymes use the other strand as a template to put back the right letters.
asks: Why does DNA have two strands?

faq.a: A mutation is a permanent change in the DNA letters. Most are harmless, some can cause problems, and over many generations a few useful mutations help living things evolve.
asks: What happens if DNA is not repaired?

faq.q: What happens if a cell is too damaged to repair?
faq.a: Cells have safety checks. If the damage is too great, the cell can stop dividing or switch on a self-destruct programme, protecting the body from a faulty cell.

facts: Each human cell can experience tens of thousands of DNA damage events a day, nearly all of which are repaired.
The 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for discoveries about how cells repair DNA.

quiz.say: How does a cell know which letters to put back after cutting out damaged DNA?
quiz.show: After cutting out damaged DNA, the cell rebuilds it using…

options.show: The matching letters on the other strand
options.say: The matching letters on the other strand

quiz.why: A pairs with T and C with G, so the undamaged strand shows exactly which letters belong in the gap.

wrong.1: Cells repair their own DNA without borrowing from neighbours.
wrong.2: Random letters would cause mutations; the template makes repair accurate.
